---
title: "Reading trace and rank plots"
execute:
  enabled: true

  warning: false

Suppose we fit the passage-level Student-t model with four independently initialized [No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)](no-u-turn-sampler.qmd) chains. How can we tell whether the chains explored the same parts of the posterior? A [**trace plot**](https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/articles/plotting-mcmc-draws.html) places iteration on the horizontal axis and a sampled quantity on the vertical axis. A **rank plot** divides the pooled ranks into bins and compares how often each chain occupies them.

All four chains are intended to sample the same [posterior distribution](posterior-distributions.qmd). The plots compare realized chain paths and rank frequencies; they do not estimate posterior variance by treating initialization as an empirical study factor. [Variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) retains its expected squared-deviation meaning whether it describes the target or a diagnostic summary.

Multiple chains begin from dispersed states so that persistent dependence on initialization can become visible. If every chain starts from the same point, agreement may merely reproduce that common start. Warmup allows each chain to move away from its initialization while Stan adapts the step size and [mass matrix](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd), which sets the scale and orientation used for HMC's simulated momentum. The displayed traces begin only after that adaptation ends.

We will read the traces as time-ordered paths and then compare the pooled rank histograms. These pictures can reveal some failures directly. They also raise questions that require the numerical diagnostics on the following pages.

## Traces from the fitted model {#production-traces}

The following code reads the retained draws from the fitted passage-level
model. It keeps chain identity and post-warmup iteration explicit, so every
plotted path follows one of the four adapted chains.

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-production-traces
library(ggplot2)
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)
draws <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(subset_draws(
  cache$production_draws, variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)))
trace_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(chain = draws$.chain, iteration = draws$.iteration,
             parameter = "mu", value = draws$mu),
  data.frame(chain = draws$.chain, iteration = draws$.iteration,
             parameter = "sigma", value = draws$sigma)
)

stopifnot(nrow(provo) == 55L, nrow(draws) == 4000L,
          length(unique(draws$.chain)) == 4L)
aggregate(value ~ parameter + chain, trace_long, mean)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-production-traces
#| fig-cap: "Four post-warmup NUTS traces from the fitted passage-level Student-t model."
trace_opacity <- .65
ggplot(trace_long,
       aes(iteration, value, group = factor(chain), color = factor(chain))) +
  geom_line(alpha = trace_opacity, linewidth = .3) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_grey(start = .15, end = .7) +
  labs(x = "Post-warmup NUTS iteration", y = "Draw", color = "Chain") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A useful trace fluctuates around a stable location, overlaps across chains, and continues to move. The passage-level Student-t model traces show these properties. They do not prove that the chains found every posterior region or that the model fits the passage summaries.

A problematic trace might show one chain staying above the others, all chains drifting together, or long nearly flat stretches. A useful-looking trace removes those visible warnings only. All chains could still occupy the same incomplete mode, and no trace plot asks whether replicated passage contrasts resemble the observed ones.

## Rank histograms

Chain identity should not systematically predict pooled rank. The code computes 20 bins for each parameter.

The pooling step ranks all 4,000 values for one parameter together. Each rank then keeps its original chain label. If the chains sample the same marginal distribution, each chain should contribute similar counts across low, middle, and high rank bins; systematic excesses reveal location, scale, or tail differences.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-rank-histograms
rank_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("mu", "sigma"), function(parameter) {
  values <- draws[[parameter]]
  ranks <- rank(values, ties.method = "average")
  bins <- cut(ranks, breaks = seq(0, length(values), length.out = 21L),
              include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)
  counts <- as.data.frame(table(chain = draws$.chain, bin = bins))
  names(counts)[3] <- "count"
  counts$parameter <- parameter
  counts
}))

stopifnot(sum(rank_rows$count) == 2L * nrow(draws))
head(rank_rows)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-rank-histograms
#| fig-cap: "Pooled-rank histograms for the fitted passage-level Student-t chains."
ggplot(rank_rows,
       aes(as.numeric(as.character(bin)), count, fill = factor(chain))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = .85) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_grey(start = .2, end = .8) +
  labs(x = "Pooled-rank bin", y = "Draws", fill = "Chain") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Persistent chain separation would suggest that initialization still predicts the sampled value. Drift would suggest that the finite saved sequence changes with iteration. Long nearly constant stretches would show inefficient movement. These are computational warnings, not model checks.

Warmup is not an arbitrary deletion of inconvenient draws. Stan uses it to adapt the step size and mass matrix, then samples with a fixed transition. Removing part of a problematic saved trace until it looks stable is not a repair.

## Recap and forward link

1. Dispersed initializations make residual starting-state effects easier to see.
2. Trace plots display movement through iteration; pooled-rank plots compare the sampled marginal distributions across chains.
3. Good-looking plots do not prove complete exploration or model adequacy.
4. Warmup adapts computation and precedes the fixed retained transition.

The [$\widehat R$ page](rhat.qmd#the-basic-variance-ratio) turns cross-chain comparison into a numerical diagnostic.

## Check your understanding

1. What does persistent chain separation show directly?
2. What additional information does a rank plot provide?
3. Why can overlapping traces still miss a posterior region?
4. Which diagnostic asks whether the passage-level Student-t model reproduces passage-level data features?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Persistent chain separation shows that chain identity or initialization continues to predict sampled values, a direct sign of incomplete cross-chain mixing. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A rank plot shows whether each chain occupies the pooled distribution's ranks similarly, revealing location, scale, or tail differences that traces can obscure. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. All chains can overlap within the same incomplete region if none reaches another posterior mode or tail. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. A posterior predictive check asks whether the passage-level Student-t model reproduces selected passage-level data features. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
